The Government cannot be congratulated on the terms of its letter to the Head of the Sanitary Board regarding the request for a children's playground for Kowloon: The letter is terseness itself. A business House could not be more cold, precise, or seemingly indifferent, even if it tried. The English language is not so poor that it cannot be plumbed for words to express a semblance of real regret in a matter which concerns the welfare and well being of quite young people. A request for a playground came from a medical man; a representative of Kowloon interests on the Sanitary Board; and the request was backed up by facts of an undisputed kind known to all who have even but a faint knowledge of Kowloon and its needs. Yet in a letter of 33 words—some devoted to the usual cliches of letter writing, the Government "regrets" that "it has no site available for a children's playground in Kowloon." The Government found a site for a religious building; it found a site for a golf course; sites for playing pitches for adults; it should have no difficulty in finding something for the many children in Kowloon. A system of building laws allows the erection of flats and houses with breathing and moving space of a low mini-

the proverbial cat, and children are crowded to the gutter," the prey of passing vehicles. The matter should not be allowed to rest with the Government's "regret"; nor at Dr. MacGown's observation that there is very little to be said about the matter in the light of the Government's letter. There is much to be said; and it is for Kowloon parents to say it.

If there is a fixed pomp about the ceremony of observing the King's birthday, it is but to remind us of the majesty that hedges in the office of kingship. It has been so from time immemorial. The ritual of the observance does not however cloak the inherent simplicity and grandeur of the kingly office. Kings
Gentlemen—The King!
..... are like stars—they rise, they set, they have The worship of the world.

But if they have not the worship of their own people set and securely fixed in affection, and devotion, they are as nothing worth. It is in the hearts of the people of Britain that the King indeed reigns by right of a conquest, simple, and unaffected, achieved with no apparent effort, but with that spirit that understands, appreciates, and enters into the lives of subjects with a perfect understanding of their own peculiar difficulties and desires. To-day's celebrations will certainly take on a distinction of their own. His Majesty has but recently recovered from an illness that but reminds us that even Kings are human and must pay tribute to the unseen. The King's birthday this year comes at a time when the heir-apparent has concluded a visit to the South African Dominion of the Crown that has been triumphal in its progress and the results of which are as apparent as later on they will be real. A younger son also returns from a visit to another part of the empire, whilst a sailor prince of still younger years remains abroad to cement the feeling that exists between the reigning house and the people of a great empire. Kings have no response; the poet Shelley tells us. Very true is this of our own King, so far as it indicates no shirking of duties, and no lack of interest in all that pertains to the welfare of his subjects. Hongkong, no less than other parts of a far-lung Empire, voices its own royalty and affection in its utterance of the simple but sincere line.

To the Communist Party must be assigned the sensation of the moment. To have smuggled into Britain two of its most noted continental leaders to attend a Conference at Glasgow, in defiance of the Government's restriction, speaks itself of the strength of the movement, and the power and determination of those who control it. How this feat of smuggling has been done, will doubtless soon be revealed. That smuggling into Britain has been going on of Communists generally has been known for sometime. It is alleged that the whole weight of the second International has been transferred from Germany to England. Not only are the Bolsheviks sending their own countrymen to Britain, but they are pressing into their service people who arrive from America travelling with United States passports. It has been found that these people are Russians naturalised as United States subjects. The incident under review is perhaps the most direct challenge which has been made to British authority—an authority which distinctly ordered that no foreign Communist was to be allowed admittance to the country to attend the Glasgow Conference. The Communist peril is directed at undermining the Constitution of the British Empire — at all costs. These "costs" include red revolution which the heart and soul of the Empire detests and is determined to subdue. Nowhere under the sun is there a more just constitution than that under which British subjects live. There is freedom and liberty for all and right means of redressing known grievances. It is not likely that the present Government will sit down lightly in face of the challenge now issued to it. It may be childish to think that a Home Secretary in his own person can stop a British revolution by preventing the Communists of different countries from meeting; but it is not childish to believe that a Home Secretary with a free Government behind him—and better still a free people—will effectively take measures to stop any undermining of such a Constitution as the British people possess, by means of anarchy. It looks very much as if the British Communist Party at any rate has voluntarily committed suicide.

S. vol. viii. p. 66) quotes from an old newspaper (June 7th, 1809) the following account of Paignton Fair, held at Exeter. At this fair, says the writer, the ancient custom of drawing through the town a plum-pudding of immense size and afterwards of distributing it to the populace, was revived on Tuesday last. The ingredients which composed this enormous pudding were — four hundred pounds of flour, one hundred and seventy pounds of beef suiet, one hundred and forty pounds of raisins, and two hundred and forty eggs. It was kept constantly boiling in a brewer's copper from Saturday morning to the Tuesday following, when it was placed on a car, decorated with ribbons, ever-greens, etc., and drawn along the streets by eight oxen.
NEW BANK SPONSOR. F o r the past few years the

signature of Sir Ernest Harvey has become familiar to all who have been fortunate enough to possess a banknote, for as chief cashier of the Bank of England a reproduction of "E. M. Harvey" appeared on every one—as a proof of its genuineness. Now Sir Edward has received promotion, and has become Comptroller in Threadneedle Street, and a new name will appear on our banknotes. His successor is Mr. C. P. Mahon, who has been deputy cashier for the past two years, and whose signature will soon be as well known as that of Sir Ernest, and his predecessor, Sir John Gordon Nairne.

This idea, which is still prevalent, was dealt with as follows by Dr. John Jones, as long ago as 1797, in his Medical and Vulgar Errors Refuted, p. 87: "Just the contrary; for it is the warm wet bath of a person's own sweat, confined by a linen shirt, which renders the heat of a warm climate so in-supportably troublesome. Flannel, by promoting perspiration, favours its evaporation and it is a well-established fact that evaporation always produces positive cold."
Modern writers on hygiene certainly recommend the wearing of a funnel next to the skin in all climates, as a wet funnel shirt is far less likely to cause a "chill" than a linen or cotton one.
Few parts of the world. SLAVES. have had a more stirring history. both for good

and evil, than the West Coast of Africa, which the Prince of Wales has explored. Here, at Sierra Leone, Drake put in on his homeward voyage round the world; here, too, Sir John Hawkins shipped his first cargo of slaves in the "Jesus"—oddly named vessel for such a trade; and here Wilberforce tried his famous experiment in colonisation with repatriated American negroes and prostitutes from the Haymaket in London. At Cape Coast Castle the slaves were branded with the initials "D. Y." for the Duke of York, patron of the famous Africa Company—Addison was once offered one of its shares as a bribe; and for three hundred years English, French, and Dutch fought each other up and down the whole West Coast for the trade in gold and ivory as well as slaves. Profits were often great, but losses were heavy, for settlers had to fight disease and death as well as the rival trader; graves were kept dug ready for use, and there used to be a grim jest in one of the West Coast colonies that the best religion was Wesleyanism, because the Wesleyans were the only sect that had a portable hearse. Tropical medicine, of course, has changed things a good deal for the better, but it is not very long since there was still point in the sailor's couplet, once famous all, over the world:
Beware, oh, beware of the Right of Benin;
THAT "D——D INDIA HOUSE."
Where few come out though many go in.

An unusual Charles Lamb centenary was celebrated by a distinguished company at dinner at the Inner Temple Hall recently under the chair-manship of Mr. Augustine Birrell, writes the London corres.
One hundred years ago “Elia,” after 33 years as an India House clerk, became “superannulated man.” On his way home from Leadenhall Street upon his last day he stopped at Crabb Robinson's Chambers in the Temple to slip into the letter box a note consisting of these words: “I have left the d—d India House for ever! Give me great joy.” It was considered appropriate by some of the most distinguished of London's literary men to celebrate the centenary of this conspicuous incident in Lamb's life, notable, for one reason, because it formed the theme of one of his finest essays. “The superannulated man.”
The company included some of the best-known men of letters and the chairmanship of Mr. Birrell, the doyen of living essayist, was appropriate. The Inner Temple Hall is adjacent to Lamb's birth place at Crown Office Row.
Proposing “The Immortal Memory,” Mr. Birrell said that it enraged him beyond description to hear people speak of “the gentle, Gentleness suggested or lessive amisibility, and it was a quality which no one loved. He was a strong man, prudent, generous, and so self-denying that he was able out of his slender means to afford assistance to friends. Lamb had one family.

"I could no more feel compassionate of him than I could claim to be his equal," declared Mr. Birrell, "and as for regret, I feel none. He had one frailty, and I am almost prepared to thank heaven for it. Otherwise I would have found him, to misquote Wordsworth, 'A creature all too bright and good for human nature's daily food'."

"What nonsense all this is," declared Mr. Birrell. "How many books described as important at their birth now have the ground floor of the pit of oblivion, while how many unimportant books may be found a hundred years after, shining in the canopy of heaven with an effulgence all their own?
"The writings of Charles Lamb have installed since 1923, and today the world over are instilling into the minds of young and impressionable readers, good taste, exquisitely fine feeling and delightful humour. No young man or woman who has ever really learned to enter into the beauty of the spirit of Lamb can ever be altogether vulgar and entirely dull and vulgarity and dullness are the two chariot enemies of the English men."
